issues.item: Triggers: Military Topics: Talks about military
issues.explanation: Military-related trigger content is hard to reconcile with the indexed trauma of a child's life-threatening illness. Ambulances is coherent for medical trauma, but military topics suggests a very different trauma context and is therefore clinically implausible here.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Rumination: Revenge: ruminate about how to get even with assailant
issues.explanation: Revenge/get-even rumination implies an identifiable perpetrator or assailant. That does not fit a child's life-threatening illness trauma, which is not typically organized around interpersonal assault. This creates a cross-node/content mismatch with the trauma type.

issues.item: Pregnancy/Birth Reminders: Pregnancy, childbirth, or babies in general
issues.explanation: Pregnancy/childbirth/babies is not a clearly coherent trigger for trauma centered on a child's life-threatening illness unless the illness was specifically neonatal/perinatal, which is not indicated. In this profile it sits awkwardly alongside the more plausible medical trigger of ambulances.

issues.item: Self-Harm Distraction: I hurt myself physically to stop thinking about the event
issues.explanation: Physical self-harm used to stop thinking about the event is possible in PTSD, but here it is weakly anchored to the rest of the profile: the only triggers are situational reminders, with no corroborating threat, appraisal, or memory items suggesting the kind of overwhelming internal distress usually linked to this strategy. Given the formulation, maladaptive strategies should connect plausibly back to the listed triggers; this item is poorly matched.

vignette: The memory of that November still arrives unbidden to Arjun, sharp and suffocating. His son, then seven, had collapsed during a routine swim practice. The paramedics’ rapid assessment, the sirens, the frantic ride to St. Jude’s meant Arjun was separated from the gurney once they breached the emergency doors. Security had ordered him to remain in the waiting area while his son was wheeled toward the cardiac unit. For fourteen hours, Arjun sat on a cracked vinyl chair, watching the automatic doors slide open and shut. When a charge nurse finally asked him to step out to a nearby hotel because the ICU had strict visiting limits and he was showing signs of exhaustion, Arjun went. That first night, alone in the unfamiliar double bed at the Days Inn, he lay rigid, listening to the highway hum, certain that every distant siren meant his son’s heart had stopped. He had come to believe that solitude was synonymous with powerlessness, that if he slept and missed the call, he would never forgive himself. Over the months that followed, the hospital’s antiseptic scent, usually masked by floor wax, began to signal immediate danger. Arjun started carrying his own bottle of lavender spray, dabbing it on his wrists before leaving the house. He avoided the emergency department’s staff entrance, taking circuitous routes around the building instead. When he did attend follow-up appointments, every needle, every stethoscope, every clipped phrase from a physician sent his pulse into a frantic rhythm. He found himself asking his wife, Priya, and his primary care physician repeatedly if his own blood pressure readings were normal, if his chest was just stress, if he was truly okay. He kept asking, watching their faces for any sign of doubt. At work, where he spent his days rendering character animations in a sunlit studio in downtown Raleigh, the smell of antiseptic from the building’s new cleaning contract sparked a sudden drop in his stomach. He would immediately stand, push his chair back, and walk to the stairwell, refusing to sit until his breathing evened out. In the quiet hours before dawn, Arjun’s mind turned to the attending pediatrician, the one he had watched from the waiting room glass. He ruminated about how to get even with assailant, mapping out steps to file complaints, to hire a lawyer, to make the man face the same terror he had endured. These patterns occupied his days without merging. He mentally rehearsed worst case scenarios: his son tripping on the playground, his wife having a sudden seizure, his own heart giving out mid-render. He would run through the protocols in his head, adjusting his posture, checking his phone for the twelfth time, trying to feel prepared. His animation work suffered in the margins. Deadlines slipped because he would pause his drawing tablet, stare at the wall, and rehearse emergency calls. He missed a colleague’s birthday dinner, citing a sudden migraine, though he had simply stayed home, rehearsing how he would speak to his son’s school principal if a similar crisis returned. By the time Arjun reached his fiftieth birthday, the weight of these habits had settled into a heavy stillness. What frightened him most was the quiet that followed when he climbed into bed, the way his hands would tremble over his tablet, the way he caught himself counting the seconds between Priya’s breaths as she slept. It was the way his mind would fracture during a routine physical exam, the way he could not look away from the antiseptic smell in the studio stairwell, that finally pushed him to schedule an intake. He sat in the waiting room now, clutching his appointment card, certain that the therapist would hear only the parts of him that were broken. What he hoped for, more than anything, was a way to stop bracing for the next collapse, to sleep through the night without listening for a phone that might not ring, and to walk past a hospital without tasting copper and alcohol on his tongue.
